themes.label: Profanity and taboo/informal insults
defining_features: profanity_or_taboo_language (explicit profanity, sexualized/vulgar insults, slur-like terms)
informal_register_or_slang (colloquial crude phrasing, meme/slogan insults)
ridicule_or_mockery (derogatory labels, mocking comparisons) when paired with taboo language
themes.interpretation: Moderation-relevant because many remove-rated posts rely on explicit taboo language and demeaning address; these likely correlate with abusive/hostile tone beyond substantive political debate.

themes.label: Call to action / imperatives to change policy or mobilize
defining_features: call_to_action (imperatives to Congress/authorities or direct urging to join/support)
policy_prescription_present (advocacy instructions, legislative steps, “act now”, “stop X”)
second_person_direct_address when used as command/urging
themes.interpretation: This theme captures pro-mobilization / pro-legislation rhetoric. It spans both labels, suggesting that policy advocacy itself isn’t the sole determinant of moderation outcome; tone and other signals (insults, due-process rejection, violence-adjacent content) likely interact with it.

themes.label: Strong causal claims (cause → blame/outcome)
defining_features: causal_claim_present (explicit cause-and-effect about events or policies)
semantic_content_causal_claim_present (motive/cause assertions tied to harm or worsening)
mirror_shift_direction when used to re-assign causal blame
themes.interpretation: Many posts make definitive causal assertions (often blame-heavy). Removes may correlate with causal language paired with dehumanization, conspiratorial implication, or extreme certainty.

themes.label: Us-vs-them / antagonistic framing by political bloc
defining_features: us_vs_them_framing (outgroup vs in-group contrast, hypocrisy contrasts, spite-voting)
target_directionality (assigns negative traits to a group/category like “GOP”, “liberals”, “greens”, “government”)
themes.interpretation: Antagonistic bloc framing appears more often in remove-rated examples, suggesting it’s a signal for heightened conflict language (especially when combined with insults or conspiracy-style certainty).

themes.label: Conspiratorial / disinformation framing
defining_features: conspiratorial_framing (labels claims as disinformation/conspiracies, reinterprets crisis as pretext)
factual_assertion_vs_speculation when used as dismissal by “goalposts moved”/evidence absence (adjacent pattern in corpus)
themes.interpretation: Moderation-relevant because many remove-rated posts explicitly categorize events as conspiracy/disinformation or allege covert schemes; even when content is political, this pattern may push toward misinformation risk.

themes.label: Policy domain advocacy/argument clusters (guns, immigration, abortion, climate, elections)
defining_features: primary_policy_domain (guns/gun laws, elections/redistricting, climate/emissions, immigration/border/ICE, abortion, healthcare/DEI-related)
specific_event_or_bill_reference (named bills/cases like Brady Bill, Obergefell/Roe, SAVE Act/PRO Act, etc.)
themes.interpretation: Shows that political topics are distributed across both labels. Moderation outcome likely depends less on the domain itself and more on the co-occurring tone signals (profanity/antagonism) and procedural/violence-adjacent prescriptions.

themes.label: Policy certainty and cost/benefit impact arguments
defining_features: economic_cost_benefit_framing (claims about reduced income/cost increases, emissions benefits/harms)
factual_assertion_vs_speculation when paired with “100%/certainty” or evidence-dismissal contrasts (adjacent)
themes.interpretation: Impact-based reasoning (costs, jobs, emissions outcomes) appears in both labels. This suggests it’s not inherently problematic; rather, it’s the combination with hostile language or extreme prescriptions that may drive removals.

themes.label: High-emphasis / high-intensity rhetoric (punctuation, capitalization, outrage)
defining_features: high_punctuation_intensity (dense punctuation, emphatic lists)
all_caps_emphasis (ALL CAPS for emphasis, shouted claims)
emphatic_outrage (shock/exclamation, intense negativity)
themes.interpretation: High-intensity typography and outrage markers correlate more with removals, likely because they co-occur with abusive or de-escalation-resistant rhetoric.

themes.label: Targeted attacks on identifiable people/entities (named officials, politicians, outlets)
defining_features: targeted_actor_politician_or_official (specific mayor/politician named)
named_proper_nouns_density (leader/outlet density)
target_directionality (dehumanizing or moral labeling tied to a named target)
themes.interpretation: Direct personalization of attacks (specific named targets) appears in both groups but more often in removals, especially when combined with profanity, dehumanizing moral language, or extreme directives.

cross_cutting_themes: Hostility intensity stacking: profanity/taboo language (Theme 1) combined with high-emphasis rhetoric (Theme 8) and antagonistic us-vs-them framing (Theme 4).
Policy advocacy with blame certainty: call_to_action/policy_prescription_present (Theme 2) combined with causal_claim_present (Theme 3) or policy certainty via cost/benefit impacts (Theme 7).
Misinformation risk pairing: conspiratorial_framing (Theme 5) co-occurs with dense named-entity attribution and/or high-emphasis rhetoric (Themes 9 and 8).
Topic-agnostic conflict cues: Themes 4, 1, and 8 appear across multiple primary_policy_domain categories (Theme 6), suggesting moderation outcomes depend more on tone than on the policy area.
